sections.content: Intercom charged $0.99 when its AI resolved a customer problem. sections.content: McCabe linked Intercom’s past pricing problems to an unfocused strategy and a tangle of charges for seats, messages, and leads, plus tiers and gates for different customer sizes. He said simpler, more predictable, fairer pricing helped customers stick around and improved the customer relationship. Intercom reduced prices for many customers and gave away roughly $50 million in ARR rather than keep the old pricing.

sections.heading: Price for the outcome and its value
sections.content: Intercom charges 99 cents when its AI resolves a customer problem, aligning revenue with the result customers receive and assessing the agents by their resolution rate. McCabe says pricing should come from value, not costs: the company’s costs are its problem, and those costs may fall over time while margins move around. He describes the 99-cent price as a balance between earning enough and making it palatable; his practical test was that if customers would not pay 99 cents for an excellent resolution, there was no business. He also cautions that customers may value digital work less than human work, even when the digital service is better, more consistent, and always available.

sections.heading: Simplify and be willing to make trade-offs
sections.content: McCabe contrasts the outcome-based model with Intercom’s former, complicated pricing across seats, messages, and leads. His lesson is to focus the strategy and make bold choices rather than charge for every possible value metric. Intercom reduced prices for many customers to make pricing simpler, more predictable, and fairer—even giving up roughly $50 million in ARR—because he says that can help customers stay longer and create a healthier relationship. The evidence describes this as what Intercom did; it does not promise that every company should make the same revenue trade-off.

answer.summary: McCabe’s advice is to keep pricing simple and fair, charge for customer value delivered, and not base the price on your costs. Intercom settled on 99 cents per resolved ticket after deciding that a customer unwilling to pay that much meant there was no business.

sections.heading: Price for an outcome, not access or internal costs
sections.content: Intercom charged 99 cents when its AI resolved a customer problem, aligning revenue with the value delivered; resolution rate was the metric used to assess the agents. McCabe said to set pricing based on value rather than costs: costs are the company’s problem, and they expected those costs to fall. He described 99 cents as the minimum that made the business worthwhile while remaining palatable to customers. Earlier, he considered $10, $5, and $2.50 per resolution, but sensed customers might value digital work less than human work even when it was more consistent and always available.

sections.heading: Make pricing simpler and fairer
sections.content: McCabe said Intercom’s old, unfocused strategy led to a tangle of pricing metrics—seats, messages, and leads, plus tiers for different customer sizes. The company simplified pricing and cut prices for many customers, giving up roughly $50 million in ARR. His rationale: simpler, more predictable, fairer pricing can help customers stick around and foster a healthier relationship. In combination, his advice is to focus the business and choose a clear value metric rather than layering on charges in every direction.
